In the plain of Hauran there was a village of black stone, surrounded by fields of wheat. That year the rain came at the right time, and the wheat grew so tall that it covered the boys when they walked into it.

When harvest came, Abu Amjad's threshing floor had the highest pile of all. Amjad climbed to the top of it and shouted to the boys, "Look! Our pile is higher than your houses!"

One of the boys said to him, "May Allah bless it for you."

Amjad said as he climbed down, "That's because Allah loves us more than everyone else. Can't you see? He gave us what He didn't give you."

The boys went quiet, and none of them knew what to say.

In the village there was a boy named Ma'n. His father had died when he was little, so he and his mother walked behind the harvesters, picking up the ears of wheat that fell.

Ma'n came close to Abu Amjad's threshing floor to pick up grains scattered on the ground, and Amjad shouted at him, "Go away, Ma'n! This is our wheat!" Ma'n got up and left without saying a word.

Then Abu Amjad's storeroom filled up with sacks of wheat. Every evening Amjad counted them and felt happy.

In winter, Ma'n knocked on the door and said, "My mother says: Will you sell us a measure of flour? We will pay you after the harvest." Amjad said, "We have nothing to sell," and shut the door. His father was not at home.

When spring came, the fields turned green, and the people of the village were happy with their crops.

Then one afternoon the sky grew dark, and hail came down, white stones the size of chickpeas. It beat down on the hillside where Abu Amjad's field was, and passed lightly over the other fields.

When the sky was calm again, Amjad went out to the field with his father. The ears of wheat lay broken in the mud.

His father stood for a long time without speaking. Then he said, "Praise be to Allah in every situation," and went back home.

Amjad sat on the stone wall crying, and said to himself, "Allah is angry with us. He honored us last year, and He has humiliated us this year."

Then Ma'n came and sat beside him. He took a small loaf of bread out of his pocket, broke it in two, and gave him half.

Amjad looked at the bread and didn't take it. He said, "Didn't I chase you away from the threshing floor?"

Ma'n said, "When my father died, I thought Allah didn't love me. Then my mother said to me: Ma'n, Allah gives and holds back to see what we will do. Being rich is a test, and being poor is a test."

Amjad took the half loaf and was quiet. He remembered the sacks of wheat he used to count, and the door he had shut.

Then he went to his father and told him everything. His father said, "There is some left in the storeroom from last year. Carry a sack of it to Umm Ma'n, as a gift, not for sale." Amjad carried it on his back and hurried off.

When harvest came the next year, Amjad left the edge of the field uncut and said to Ma'n, "This is for you and your mother."

﴿فَأَمَّا الْإِنسَانُ إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ رَبُّهُ فَأَكْرَمَهُ وَنَعَّمَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ ۝ وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ ۝ كَلَّا ۖ بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ ۝ وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ﴾

📖 Al-Fajr 15–18. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
